items.title: Level Up Lebanon Wraps Biggest Season Yet
items.desc: Wards 1 and 4 residents brought roughly 200 cars’ worth of cleanup to this fall’s Level Up Lebanon — see the numbers.
items.body: Lebanon's Level Up program just closed out its best season yet. "It is amazing what we can accomplish when a community comes together with a common purpose," said Code Administration Director Christina Dowden. "It takes teamwork, dedication, and community pride to make a program like this successful, and Lebanon has certainly shown all three." Level Up Lebanon runs twice a year. Wards 2 and 3 are up next in the spring. The program is open to Lebanon residents looking to clear out unwanted items, and the City plans to continue it in 2027. Questions about the next round? Email leveluplebanon@lebanonmo.org or call (417) 991-3905.

items.body: An Endangered Silver Advisory Alert issued over the weekend by Osage Beach police is short-lived. The alert was issued at 2:00 Saturday afternoon at 4252 U.S. 54 for a 78-year-old man who has a history of stroke. The man was apparently located during the evening hours and was described as safe and the alert was canceled.

items.title: Athlete of the Week: Johnny Carriger, Crocker Soccer
items.desc: Share on Facebook Share on Twitter As an underclassman, Johnny Carriger was ready for the moment, scoring a hat trick in Crocker’s district championship game. “I think we just wanted it more,” Johnny said. “They came out
items.body: As an underclassman, Johnny Carriger was ready for the moment, scoring a hat trick in Crocker’s district championship game. “I think we just wanted it more,” Johnny said. “They came out like they were going to win. They went up 2-0 in the first half, and I was like someone’s got to step up. So I did.” It was his second hat trick of the tournament, all while battling illness and injury. “He had a 103 fever at district time to send us to the final,” said Crocker Head Soccer Coach Rich Heenan. “Two weeks prior he had broke his hand and powered through without anything on his hand. [Johnny] played the rest of the season in a full cast.” On top of toughness, scoring goals runs in the family. His older brother, Tristen, put up Laquey’s lone goal in the Hornet’s state semifinal game. Johnny was there watching in the stands. “Whenever he scored it I was like dang, why couldn’t that be me,” Johnny said. Now, Tristen is Crocker’s assistant soccer coach. “I just cannot call him coach,” Johnny said. “It’s just too funny.” “He’s watched me play for years,” Tristen Carriger said. “But now it’s me watching him play.” Johnny is nearing 100 career goals as a varsity starter. 34 of them are in the last 16 games. Tristen gets a front-row view of his brother’s success and more. “He likes to help his teammates and help them figure out how to pass the ball better [or] how to do a soccer move,” Tristen said. “[He] even leads them to getting their first goal.” Johnny has no plans of slowing his scoring spree, but as his brother would wan, he’s turned into a leader on top of a striker.

items.title: Rockin’ Rogersville Grows Into Community Festival
items.desc: What started as a night of live music in Rogersville has grown into something quite a bit bigger. The ninth annual Rockin’ Rogersville brought music, food, local vendors and a […]
items.body: What started as a night of live music in Rogersville has grown into something quite a bit bigger. The ninth annual Rockin’ Rogersville brought music, food, local vendors and a new kids’ area together this year, all while raising money that will eventually make its way back into the community. The event is the signature fundraiser for the Community Foundation of Rogersville, an affiliate of the Community Foundation of the Ozarks. Christina Craig, board president of the Community Foundation of Rogersville, said the event has continued to change as organizers listen to what people want. “When it originally started, it was like a rock concert,” Craig said. The early version featured local bands, food trucks, and an evening fireworks show. This year looked a little different. Organizers added a vendor marketplace with 33 vendors, giving local artisans and crafters a chance to show and sell their work. Nine food trucks were also part of the event. A new kids’ zone helped move Rockin’ Rogersville even further toward becoming a full family festival. “We’re kind of trying to make it more of a family-centered event,” Craig said. “So not just a rock concert, but more of a festival.” Music is still a big part of it. Five bands performed this year, including KC and the Atta Boys, the Stephen James Gang, Dawson Hollow, Isaac Kenneth Band and KC Flo. Instead of sticking with one type of music, organizers mixed things up. Craig said previous years have leaned heavily toward either country or rock. This year’s lineup offered a little bluegrass, country, rockabilly, and rock. The foundation uses feedback from those attending to help decide what people would like to hear at future events. items.title: Shine Through Faith Brings Helping Hands to Marshfield
items.desc: Sometimes, helping someone doesn’t take much. It might be mowing a yard, picking up groceries, or simply making sure an elderly neighbor has someone to turn to. That’s the idea […]
items.body: Sometimes, helping someone doesn’t take much. It might be mowing a yard, picking up groceries, or simply making sure an elderly neighbor has someone to turn to. That’s the idea behind Shine Through Faith, a Marshfield nonprofit founded by Heather Rodriguez. What started as a way to help older residents remain in their homes has grown into a community resource center helping families, foster children, teachers, and others who need a hand. For Rodriguez, the organization grew out of some difficult times in her own life. She has spent much of her life between Missouri and Arizona. Her grandparents lived in Missouri, and she raised her daughters here for much of their childhood. After spending more time in Arizona, she and her family returned to Missouri so their younger boys could grow up here, too. Rodriguez has always enjoyed volunteering and helping others. But after being diagnosed with thyroid cancer and having to medically retire, she found herself wondering what came next. “I thought everything was over,” she said. During that time, Rodriguez said she felt God leading her toward something called Shine Through Faith. She just wasn’t sure what it was supposed to become. About five years later, after meeting several elderly people who had little or no family support, the answer began to take shape. “I was like, how can I make a difference with them?” she said. That question became the starting point for Shine Through Faith. The original mission was simple: help elderly residents stay in their own homes longer by connecting them with volunteers who could handle everyday tasks.
